structure.title: Acts I–II · A bedroom in Britain, a wager in Rome
structure.text: Imogen's father banishes her husband. Once abroad, Posthumus accepts a stranger's wager about the wife he has just had to leave. Iachimo's journey puts the audience on both sides of the sea. We see how he obtains his information before we hear the use he makes of it in Rome.

structure.title: Acts III–IV · Messages lead people out of court
structure.text: A letter can cross the distance between Italy and Britain more easily than a husband and wife can question one another. Orders, promises and disguises draw the action towards Wales. A cave offers a princess a kind of hospitality she has had little reason to expect from people in her father's palace.

structure.title: Act V · A battlefield brings strangers into one another's stories
structure.text: Britain and Rome have a quarrel of their own over tribute. Once armies meet, people travelling for intensely private reasons find themselves at the same encounter. The audience has had the privilege of following several journeys. The characters must still work out whose story each of them has wandered into.

people.name: Imogen
people.text: She has already defied the king by marrying the man she trusts. An extraordinary amount of the plot then proceeds through other people speaking about her in rooms from which she is absent. Her own resourcefulness becomes easier to see once she has to travel and decide whose help to accept.

people.name: Posthumus and Iachimo
people.role: The husband who wagers and the stranger who takes him up
people.text: Posthumus regards his certainty about Imogen as a compliment to her. Iachimo sees that he can turn it into a contest between men. They discuss the value of a ring and a woman's fidelity together, without asking who gave either man the right to put the latter at stake.

people.name: Pisanio
people.role: A servant trusted on both sides of the separation
people.text: Pisanio can carry a letter, read one and decide what obedience to its sender would actually involve. The service expected from him becomes a matter of judgment precisely because his master has such confidence that his words will be obeyed.

context.title: What a piece of evidence can establish
context.text: A stranger who knows the furnishings in someone's bedroom might sound persuasive when he claims to know its occupant intimately. Those facts can have different causes. The play takes the trouble to show both the acquisition of a detail and the situation in which another person is asked to believe it.

notice.text: Follow the bracelet and ring when the lovers part.
notice.why: At first their value belongs to a private exchange between two people. In another room, an object can be displayed to a man who has no idea how it got there. The audience remembers the feeling attached to it while watching it acquire a quite different evidential value.

passages.quote: Puts a bracelet on her arm.

notice.text: Listen to what Imogen hears when someone says Milford Haven.
notice.why: For a military commander it is a place on a map. For Imogen it holds a promise about a person she hopes to see. A name can pull the courtship plot and the war plot along the same road while the people travelling it have different destinations in mind.

opening: Imogen marries against her father's wishes, trusting a husband whose confidence in her will soon be put to a grotesque test. Another man wagers that he can prove her unfaithful. He does not need to win her affection if he can manufacture evidence convincing enough to send abroad. Shakespeare sets the intimate danger inside a Britain of court plots, disguises, and threatened war. The adventures multiply around a simple injury: someone who claims to love a woman may find a stranger's account of her easier to believe.
